title: Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator: $25,000+ Funding, Mentorship and Global Support for Early-Stage Tech Nonprofits
summary: The Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator is an opportunity for early-stage technology nonprofits using innovative digital solutions to address major social, environmental, health, education, economic, or humanitarian challenges. The programme is designed to help promising tech nonprofits strengthen their organizations, improve their technology and products, access philanthropic capital, develop sustainable growth strategies, and connect with a powerful global community of founders, funders, technology professionals, and social-impact leaders. Applications for the 2027 cohort open on August 17, 2026 , and close on September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time (PT) . Fast Forward describes itself as an organization focused on helping entrepreneurs apply the best of technology to some of the world s biggest social problems. Through its Accelerator and wider ecosystem of resources, the organization brings together the technology, nonprofit, and philanthropic sectors to help technology-driven nonprofits move from early-stage development toward sustainable scale. According to Fast Forward, it has accelerated 112+ tech nonprofits , which have collectively gone on to impact more than 415 million lives and raise more than $1.4 billion in follow-on funding . About the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator The Fast Forward Accelerator is the organization s flagship and longest-standing programme for early-stage tech nonprofits. Rather than functioning simply as a conventional grant programme, the Accelerator combines philanthropic funding, training, mentorship, community, strategic guidance, fundraising support, product development expertise, and visibility . The programme is specifically designed around the challenges faced by organizations that operate at the intersection of technology and social impact. Selected organizations receive a combination of: $25,000+ in philanthropic seed capital Tailored training and educational content Mentorship and expert guidance Access to a community of technology nonprofit founders Support with fundraising and nonprofit development Product and technology guidance Growth and scaling strategies Opportunities to connect with funders and supporters Exposure through Fast Forward s broader ecosystem Participation in Demo Days attended by a large audience of funders and supporters The programme aims to select approximately 10 teams per cohort , although Fast Forward notes that the exact number can fluctuate depending on the strength and composition of the applicant pool. What Is a Tech Nonprofit? A central requirement for this opportunity is that applicants operate as technology nonprofits. Fast Forward defines a tech nonprofit as a nonprofit organization that uses technology, including artificial intelligence, to address challenges affecting people, communities, society, or humanity more broadly. Examples can include organizations working in areas such as: Healthcare access Education and education equity Climate action Humanitarian assistance Poverty reduction Digital inclusion Public-interest technology Economic opportunity Community development Social justice Accessibility Environmental sustainability Civic participation Other major social or humanitarian challenges The defining characteristic is that technology is central to the organization s solution and social impact model . Fast Forward points to organizations such as Wikipedia and Khan Academy as examples of technology nonprofits and notes that its directory included more than 1,400 tech nonprofits worldwide as of 2026. What Support Does the Accelerator Provide? The Accelerator is structured around three major areas of support: Capital, Content, and Cohort . 1. Capital Early-stage technology nonprofits often face a difficult funding environment. Traditional nonprofit funders may not understand technology-based business models, while traditional technology investors may not be interested in organizations whose primary objective is social impact rather than financial profit. Fast Forward seeks to help bridge this gap. Participants receive $25,000 or more in seed philanthropic capital , while also gaining guidance on navigating the fundraising environment for technology nonprofits. This funding can provide an important source of early-stage capital as an organization works to strengthen its technology, team, operations, impact measurement, and growth strategy. 2. Content and Training The Accelerator provides curriculum addressing both sides of the technology nonprofit equation. On the nonprofit side, participants may receive guidance related to areas such as: Board development Impact measurement Volunteer management Fundraising Organizational development Nonprofit operations On the technology side, the programme explores topics such as: Product development Go-to-market strategy Technology leadership Scaling Growth Product strategy Sustainable expansion This combination is particularly relevant to founders who have strong technical or social-impact expertise but need support in strengthening the other side of their organization. 3. Cohort and Community Building a technology nonprofit can be challenging because founders often face problems that are different from those encountered by traditional nonprofits or conventional technology startups. The Accelerator therefore places considerable emphasis on peer learning and community. Selected founders become part of a cohort of organizations facing similar challenges. They also become part of Fast Forward s broader portfolio and ecosystem, allowing them to build relationships beyond the immediate programme. This network can provide opportunities for: Peer learning Collaboration Mentorship Knowledge exchange Strategic partnerships Fundraising connections Technology expertise Long-term community support Key Programme Timeline for the 2027 Cohort Applicants should pay close attention to the following dates and programme milestones: Programme Stage Date/Period Application Opens August 17, 2026 Application Workshop August 12, 2026, 10:00–11:00 a.m. PT Application Deadline September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. PT Interviews October–December 2026 Final Notifications By the end of 2026 Programme Begins Late February 2027 Programme Ends Early June 2027 Demo Days Late May–early June 2027 Applicants should prepare their materials well before the deadline because the application requires detailed information about the organization, its technology, its impact, its leadership, and its potential for growth. Application Deadline The application deadline for the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator is: September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time (PT). Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit. The application process may require coordination between multiple co-founders, preparation of organizational information, development of a compelling narrative, and potentially the creation or submission of video materials. Who Is Fast Forward Looking For? Fast Forward uses a holistic application review process. This means the organization does not evaluate applicants based on a single factor. The organization states that its only hard requirement is that applicants are: Early-stage tech nonprofits with at least a minimum viable product (MVP) built. Beyond this requirement, Fast Forward considers several characteristics when evaluating an organization s fit. Leadership Fast Forward looks for visionary leaders capable of navigating both the technology and nonprofit environments. Strong applicants should be able to demonstrate: A clear vision Strong understanding of the problem being addressed Leadership capability Commitment to social impact Ability to build and lead a team Willingness to learn and adapt Understanding of both technology and organizational development You do not necessarily have to be the original founder to apply. Fast Forward states that the current leader of an organization can apply. Technology Talent The organization values technology expertise within leadership teams. Applicants should ideally have mission-driven technology professionals in leadership positions or a credible plan for bringing appropriate technology talent onto the team. Fast Forward recognizes that hiring a full-time Chief Technology Officer may not be financially realistic for every early-stage organization. Therefore, organizations that outsource some software development are still encouraged to apply when their software is central to their impact. However, having strong internal technology leadership or a clear plan to establish it can strengthen an application. Impact Potential Applicants should demonstrate that their organization has the potential to make a meaningful difference. This involves clearly explaining: What problem the organization addresses Who experiences the problem Why the problem is important How the organization s solution works Why technology is necessary or particularly valuable How many people could ultimately benefit What evidence exists that the solution is working What additional impact could occur if the organization scales Scalability Fast Forward places particular emphasis on software-based solutions with significant growth potential. Applicants should therefore demonstrate that their technology can potentially serve a much larger population without requiring costs to increase at exactly the same rate as users or beneficiaries. A strong application should explain how the organization can move from its current stage toward broader adoption and impact. Lived Experience Fast Forward recognizes the value of founders and leaders who have personally experienced the problem they are trying to solve. Applicants can strengthen their case by explaining relevant lived experience and showing how that experience contributes to their understanding of the community, challenge, or problem. This does not mean every applicant must personally have experienced the problem. Rather, it demonstrates why deep understanding of the people being served is important. Alignment Fast Forward also considers whether its resources, expertise, network, and investment can make a meaningful difference to the organization. Applicants should therefore think carefully about why Fast Forward is the right accelerator for their organization at its current stage. You Do Not Have to Be a Perfect Match One of the notable aspects of Fast Forward s application guidance is its encouragement to organizations that meet most, but not necessarily every, preferred characteristic. The organization specifically encourages applicants not to self-reject simply because they do not perfectly match every criterion. This is particularly important for founders who may underestimate their competitiveness because they lack one desirable characteristic. If your organization meets the fundamental requirement of being an early-stage technology nonprofit with an MVP and has strong potential for social impact, Fast Forward encourages you to consider applying. The Accelerator Is Global The Fast Forward Accelerator is not restricted to organizations based in the United States. The programme is global and Fast Forward states that it prioritizes geographic diversity within its cohorts. Organizations based outside the United States can apply provided they meet the relevant nonprofit requirements. For example, an organization based outside the U.S. does not necessarily need to possess U.S. 501(c)(3) status. Fast Forward states that organizations can apply if they are registered as nonprofits in their own countries . This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to technology nonprofits across Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, the Middle East, Oceania, and other regions. Can Organizations Outside San Francisco Apply? Yes. Applicants do not need to be located in San Francisco or the Bay Area. However, participation requires attendance at certain in-person components of the programme. The Accelerator includes: An in-person kickoff in San Francisco in February In-person and virtual Demo Days in May and/or June Mostly virtual programming throughout the programme Fast Forward provides additional travel support for teams based outside the Bay Area to help facilitate participation in required in-person activities. This means international applicants should be prepared to travel to the United States when required by the programme. Programme Time Commitment Applicants should carefully consider the time commitment before applying. Fast Forward describes the Accelerator as a major commitment . The programme is scheduled for: Tuesdays and Thursdays 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. Pacific Time Approximately three additional meeting hours each week Additional homework and preparation outside scheduled programming At least one co-founder must attend every session . Additionally, the co-founder who will pitch at Demo Day must participate in all relevant pitch practice sessions. This requirement is particularly important for international applicants because the programme schedule is based on Pacific Time. Participants in Africa, Europe, Asia, and other regions should assess the time-zone implications before applying. The Fast Forward Accelerator Is Hybrid The programme combines virtual and in-person participation. Most of the Accelerator s programming takes place virtually, making it accessible to organizations around the world. However, participants should expect in-person components, including: A kickoff in San Francisco in February 2027 In-person components associated with Demo Days Other required in-person programme activities where applicable Fast Forward provides travel assistance for teams located outside the Bay Area. The organization also states that accommodations can be provided for in-person programming weeks, although accommodations are not provided for the entire programme. Demo Days and Investor Exposure One of the major highlights of the Accelerator is Demo Day. Demo Days provide participating organizations with an opportunity to present the progress they have made during the programme to a large audience of funders and supporters. Fast Forward states that Demo Day audiences can include more than 1,000 funders and supporters . For an early-stage technology nonprofit, this can create opportunities for: Visibility Fundraising Strategic partnerships Donor relationships Ecosystem connections Future growth Increased credibility The Demo Day presentation is therefore not simply a final academic exercise. It can serve as an important opportunity for organizations to communicate their mission, demonstrate evidence of impact, present their technology, and explain their future growth strategy to potential supporters. Can an Organization Apply Without Formal U.S. Nonprofit Registration? Yes. Fast Forward states that organizations that are not yet formally registered as nonprofits may still apply, and the organization can provide assistance with the incorporation process. For organizations outside the United States, Fast Forward states that they can apply without a U.S. 501(c)(3) designation as long as they are registered as nonprofits in their own country. This makes the programme more accessible to international nonprofit organizations. Can Organizations Without an MVP Apply? No. Having a minimum viable product (MVP) is the fundamental hard requirement identified by Fast Forward. Organizations that are still at the idea, concept, or research stage are therefore not yet eligible for the Accelerator. However, Fast Forward recommends that early-stage teams without an MVP make use of its technology nonprofit resources and playbooks to develop their ideas toward implementation. This distinction is important: the Accelerator is designed for organizations that have progressed beyond the idea stage and already have a working MVP. What If Software Development Is Outsourced? Organizations that outsource software development can still apply. Fast Forward prefers organizations with internal technology leadership or plans to hire a Chief Technology Officer in the near future, but recognizes that early-stage organizations may not have sufficient resources to maintain a large internal technical team. The key consideration is whether software is central to the organization s impact . Therefore, applicants that rely on external developers should clearly explain: Why technology is central to the mission How the software is developed and maintained Who owns the product and technical vision How technical decisions are made Whether the organization plans to develop internal technical capacity How the technology will scale Additional Resources Available Through Fast Forward The Accelerator is only one component of Fast Forward s wider support ecosystem. Tech Nonprofit Tools Fast Forward provides guides and resources covering areas such as: Scaling Fundraising Product design Revenue Organizational development Technology nonprofit strategy These resources are particularly useful for organizations that are not yet ready for the Accelerator. Tech Nonprofit Directory Fast Forward operates a directory of technology nonprofits designed to increase their visibility among: Funders Potential employees Advisors Partners Other ecosystem stakeholders Being part of a broader technology nonprofit ecosystem can help organizations become more discoverable. Tech Nonprofit Job Board Fast Forward also maintains a job board featuring opportunities from technology nonprofits. Organizations can use the platform to find mission-driven talent, while technology professionals can discover employment opportunities in the social-impact sector. Funding Forward Funding Forward is a weekly newsletter featuring information about: Grant opportunities Events Resources Articles Opportunities relevant to social entrepreneurs For organizations that are not yet ready for the Accelerator, following Fast Forward s funding resources can help them identify future opportunities. What s Good in Tech Fast Forward s monthly What s Good in Tech communication highlights developments within the Fast Forward ecosystem and the broader technology-for-good sector. AI for Humanity The organization also provides a monthly newsletter focused on AI-powered nonprofits and developments in the use of artificial intelligence for social impact. Fast Forward s Broader Areas of Focus Fast Forward s work is organized around several strategic priorities. 1. Building the Pipeline Fast Forward seeks to expand the technology nonprofit sector by supporting a diverse pipeline of high-impact and community-driven builders. 2. Launching Promising Builders The Accelerator serves as the organization s flagship mechanism for supporting promising early-stage technology nonprofit organizations. 3. Supporting Scale Fast Forward also supports nonprofits that have progressed beyond the startup stage and require guidance to become larger and more influential organizations. 4. Strengthening the Ecosystem The organization works with leaders throughout the technology-for-good ecosystem to increase access to capital, resources, expertise, and visibility. 5. Maximizing AI for Social Impact Fast Forward is also focused on helping nonprofits use artificial intelligence to strengthen their missions and increase their potential social impact. Fast Forward s Funding and Partnership Ecosystem Fast Forward is a U.S. 501(c)(3) organization and works with technology companies, philanthropic foundations, and other supporters. Its listed supporters include organizations and foundations such as Google.org, BlackRock, The HPE Foundation, Ballmer Group, Bloomberg, Salesforce, Okta, Patrick J. McGovern Foundation, Twilio.org, ServiceNow, Dell Technologies, Reid Hoffman, Deloitte Health Equity Institute, The William Flora Hewlett Foundation, Splunk, Pinterest, eBay Foundation, The Equinix Foundation, The UPS Foundation, Akamai Foundation, GitLab Foundation, Comcast Business, OpenAI, HubSpot, New Relic, and Docusign, among others. This broader ecosystem is one of the potential advantages for Accelerator participants because the programme connects technology nonprofits with organizations operating across technology, philanthropy, finance, and social impact. Application Process The application process is designed to help Fast Forward understand the organization, its leadership, technology, social problem, and potential for scale. Applicants should expect to provide information about areas such as: The organization and its mission The social problem being addressed The target population The technology or software solution The current MVP Evidence of progress and impact Leadership and team capabilities Technology expertise Growth and scalability Funding and organizational development Future plans Why Fast Forward is the right fit Fast Forward provides a dedicated application page containing the application questions, character limits, and guidance for preparing responses. Applicants should review the questions before beginning the final submission so they can develop coherent and consistent answers across the entire application. Application Review and Use of Artificial Intelligence Fast Forward states that it uses artificial intelligence to assist with reviewing applications. However, applicants should understand that AI does not make the final decision . According to Fast Forward, every application is read and decided by its team. This means applicants should focus on communicating their organization s story, evidence, technology, leadership, and potential impact clearly rather than attempting to optimize their application for an automated system. Interviews Applicants who progress in the selection process will participate in an interview. Fast Forward states that selected applicants may participate in a 40-minute interview with its team. The organization may also contact applicants by email during the application period if clarification is needed. Interviews are expected to take place between October and December 2026 . Final notifications are expected by the end of 2026 . Video Requirements Fast Forward may request video material as part of the application. Applicants can submit a Zoom recording or combine video clips from individual co-founders. This means teams do not necessarily need sophisticated video-production equipment. The most important consideration should be communicating the organization s mission and value proposition clearly and authentically. Reapplying Is Allowed Organizations that apply but are not selected should not necessarily consider the process a dead end. Fast Forward encourages organizations to reapply. The organization notes that some teams apply for multiple years before eventually becoming a strong fit for the programme. This means applicants can use an unsuccessful application as a learning opportunity, strengthen their MVP, demonstrate additional impact, improve their leadership team, develop stronger technology capacity, and apply again in a future cycle. How to Prepare a Strong Application Although Fast Forward evaluates applications holistically, applicants can improve their submission by clearly demonstrating several critical elements. Demonstrate a Real Problem Do not simply state that a problem exists. Explain its scale, consequences, affected populations, and why existing approaches are insufficient. Explain the Technology Clearly The application should make it easy for reviewers to understand what the technology does and how it addresses the identified problem. Avoid unnecessary technical jargon. Prove That an MVP Exists Because an MVP is a hard requirement, applicants should clearly demonstrate that they have progressed beyond an idea. Where possible, explain: What has been built Who is using it What users are saying What has been learned What has changed based on feedback What remains to be developed Show Evidence of Impact Quantitative and qualitative evidence can help demonstrate progress. This might include: Number of users Number of beneficiaries Adoption rates Retention Outcomes Testimonials Partnerships Pilot results Geographic reach Measurable improvements Explain Why You Can Scale Do not simply claim that the organization is scalable. Explain how the technology can reach a much larger population and what resources will be needed to achieve that growth. Highlight the Team Explain why the leadership team is capable of solving the problem. Show the combination of: Technical expertise Sector knowledge Leadership Community understanding Entrepreneurial ability Lived experience Commitment to the mission Explain Why Fast Forward A strong application should also explain why the Accelerator is needed at this particular stage. Applicants should identify the specific gaps Fast Forward can help address, whether those gaps involve fundraising, product strategy, scaling, nonprofit development, technology leadership, impact measurement, or access to networks. Important Considerations for International Applicants International applicants should carefully assess the programme s requirements before applying. Although the Accelerator is global, selected organizations must be able to participate in required in-person activities in San Francisco. Applicants outside the Bay Area should therefore consider: International travel requirements Visa and entry requirements Time-zone differences Availability of at least one co-founder Participation in Tuesday and Thursday sessions Additional weekly meetings Programme homework Attendance at Demo Day Travel logistics Fast Forward provides travel assistance for teams outside the Bay Area, but applicants should still plan carefully for international participation. Who Can Apply? The opportunity is primarily intended for: Early-stage technology nonprofits Nonprofit organizations using software or technology as a central part of their impact model Organizations that already have a minimum viable product Organizations with strong potential for social impact Organizations with software-based solutions capable of scaling U.S.-based nonprofit organizations International nonprofits registered in their respective countries Current organizational leaders, including leaders who are not the original founder Teams with strong technology leadership or a credible plan to build technical capacity Fast Forward does not restrict the Accelerator to a particular race, nationality, or continent. The programme is global and explicitly seeks geographic diversity within its cohorts. Organizations from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, the Middle East, and other regions may therefore be considered, provided they satisfy the programme s requirements. For organizations outside the United States, Fast Forward states that formal U.S. 501(c)(3) status is not required where the organization is properly registered as a nonprofit in its own country. APPLY HERE Who Is Not Eligible? The following organizations may not be suitable for the 2027 Accelerator: Individuals applying without an organization Conventional for-profit startups Organizations without a technology-centered solution Teams that only have an idea and no MVP Organizations still exclusively in the research or concept stage Organizations where software is not central to the impact model Fast Forward specifically focuses on tech nonprofits , so applicants should ensure that the connection between their technology and social impact is clear. How to Apply Applicants should carefully review the official application questions, character limits, and application guidance before preparing their submission. Applicants should also review the Fast Forward website and official programme information for any updates before submitting their application. Visit HERE to learn more about the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator. Application Deadline The deadline to apply for the Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator is: September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time (PT). Applicants are strongly encouraged to submit before the final day to avoid technical problems, time-zone confusion, or incomplete application materials. Conclusion The Fast Forward 2027 Accelerator represents a significant opportunity for early-stage technology nonprofits seeking to move from promising innovation toward sustainable scale. With $25,000+ in philanthropic seed funding , specialized training, mentorship, peer community, fundraising guidance, technology and product support, and access to a broad ecosystem of funders and supporters, the programme goes beyond financial assistance. It is designed to help organizations strengthen the foundations required to become high-impact, scalable technology nonprofits. The opportunity is particularly relevant to organizations that have already built an MVP and can demonstrate that their technology addresses a significant social or humanitarian problem. International organizations are welcome, and applicants do not need to be based in San Francisco or hold U.S. 501(c)(3) status, provided they meet the applicable nonprofit requirements. However, applicants should take the programme s time commitment seriously. At least one co-founder must participate in the sessions, the programme includes additional weekly work, and participants must be prepared to attend required in-person activities in San Francisco. For technology nonprofit founders with a functioning MVP, strong social-impact ambitions, and a clear pathway toward scale, this could be an important opportunity to gain the capital, knowledge, relationships, and visibility needed to take their organization to the next level. Application deadline: September 7, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. PT. title: 2027 Guggenheim Fellowships in USA and Canada | Funding for Mid-Career Professionals
summary: The John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation has released new, user-friendly resources to help prospective applicants determine whether the Guggenheim Fellowship is the right opportunity for them at this stage of their careers. The Guggenheim Fellowship supports exceptional mid-career professionals across a wide range of fields , including individuals working with or without university affiliations. The Foundation has also published a detailed application guide and video explaining the application process, selection procedure, and materials required. About the Guggenheim Fellowship The Guggenheim Fellowship is designed for established professionals who have demonstrated significant achievement in their fields and have a strong project they are ready to pursue. The Foundation emphasizes that “mid-career” is determined by a candidate’s professional record and output rather than age or institutional affiliation . Recent Fellows have ranged from their late twenties to their late seventies. Applicants should have: A significant and recognized record of achievement in their field. A clear and well-defined project they are ready to undertake. The professional experience and record necessary to complete the proposed project at a high level of excellence. Students and individuals who have not yet established a significant record of achievement are generally not considered strong candidates. Eligibility To be eligible for the 2027 Guggenheim Fellowship, applicants must: Be citizens or permanent residents of the United States or Canada . Be mid-career professionals , with or without university affiliations. Not have previously received a Guggenheim Fellowship . Applicants do not need to hold a university position. Independent professionals without institutional affiliations are considered on an equal footing. The Foundation states that what matters most is the strength of the applicant’s record, the merits of the proposed project, and their readiness to complete it to the highest degree of excellence. How the Selection Process Works Every application is reviewed by hand. The selection process takes more than six months and is conducted by experts selected by the Foundation from among former Guggenheim Fellowship recipients. Each application is assessed in full by two to five reviewers . The strongest applicants are recommended to the interdisciplinary Committee of Selection, which must reach consensus before an applicant advances. Final awards are confirmed by the Foundation’s Board of Trustees. The identities of reviewers and jurors remain confidential. Application Requirements Applicants must complete several sections through the online application portal. Applicant Information Applicants will provide information including: Contact information Project information Addresses Employment history Languages Professional memberships Education Supporting Documents Three major documents are required: Career Narrative – maximum 1,000 words or approximately four pages. Most Significant Works – up to seven works. Statement of Plans – maximum 1,000 words or approximately four pages. Applicants must also provide three references , with a fourth reference permitted. Career Narrative The Career Narrative should explain why the applicant is the right person to complete the proposed project. It should tell the story of the applicant’s career, including what led them to the proposed project, how the project fits into their professional development, and how it connects to their broader goals. The Career Narrative should not simply be a CV or list of accomplishments . Statement of Plans The Statement of Plans should present a clear proposal for a single project that the applicant is prepared to pursue. Applicants should explain: What they want to accomplish and why the project matters. The current stage of the project. What they can realistically accomplish during the six- to twelve-month Fellowship period. Why they are capable of undertaking the proposed work. The statement should be persuasive to both specialists in the applicant’s field and non-specialists serving on the Committee of Selection. Applicants should not include a budget or financial details in the Statement of Plans. References Applicants must provide three references and may provide a fourth . References should be individuals who know the applicant and their work well enough to speak persuasively about their abilities, particularly in relation to the proposed project. References do not have to be Guggenheim Fellows. Applicants are advised to obtain permission from their references before listing them and ensure that they understand the submission timeline. Work Examples Depending on the proposed field, applicants may also need to submit work examples. Requirements vary significantly by field. For example, Fine Arts and Photography applicants may submit up to 20 digital images and/or up to three links to time-based media, while Film-Video applicants can submit links to up to three full-length works. Applicants should carefully review the requirements for their particular field before submitting work examples. Application Document Requirements Supporting documents must: Be in 12-point standard fonts . Be double-spaced . Be submitted as PDFs . Be unsecured and not password protected. Use portrait orientation. Be no larger than 5 MB per document. Deadline September 29, 2026 All required work examples must be submitted or postmarked by September 29, 2026 . Applicants should also make sure they complete the final submission process. Simply completing the application is not enough; applicants must select “ Final Submit Application ” before the deadline for their application to be considered. Important Warning for Applicants The John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation specifically advises applicants to be cautious about external consultants who claim to have special access to the Fellowship selection process. The Foundation does not endorse external consultants and states that individuals who charge a fee do not have inside information about or influence over Fellowship selection. The best way to understand the Fellowship is to use the Foundation’s own application materials, video resources, and official guidance. Applicants with questions are encouraged to contact the Foundation directly. How to Apply The 2027 Guggenheim Fellowship application is available through the official application portal. Application Portal: https://competition.gf.org/signin Applicants can create a new account or use an existing account from the previous competition. Conclusion The Guggenheim Fellowship offers established professionals an opportunity to pursue ambitious work with the support and recognition of one of the most respected fellowship programs in the United States and Canada. If you believe your professional record, proposed project, and achievements make you a strong candidate, take time to study the Foundation’s official materials and prepare your application carefully before the deadline. title: CPHIA 2026 in Addis Ababa: Register for Africa CDC’s 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa
summary: The 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026) will take place from 23–27 November 2026 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia , bringing together public health leaders, researchers, policymakers, governments, private-sector actors, innovators, programme implementers, and partners from across Africa and the wider global health community. The conference is co-hosted by the Government of Ethiopia and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) . CPHIA is Africa CDC’s flagship annual public health conference and has grown into an important continental platform for discussing the health challenges facing Africa, sharing scientific evidence and innovations, building partnerships, and turning research into policies, health products, programmes, and practical action. The theme for the 2026 edition is: “Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from health dependency and vulnerability to ownership and resilience.” CPHIA 2026 is expected to feature five days of high-level policy dialogue, scientific sessions, research presentations, innovation showcases, partnership development, networking, awards, exhibitions, and opportunities for organizations to host side events. The official conference website states that more than 30,000 attendees are expected . Researchers also have an opportunity to submit abstracts for presentation at the conference. The current official abstract submission deadline is 15 September 2026 , while early-bird conference registration is scheduled to close on 22 August 2026 . About the International Conference on Public Health in Africa The International Conference on Public Health in Africa, widely known as CPHIA , is a flagship Africa CDC platform bringing together stakeholders across different levels of the health sector. The conference connects: Political leaders Policymakers Scientists Researchers Public health professionals Programme implementers Private-sector representatives Community actors Innovators Development partners Government institutions Global health organizations Its purpose is not simply to provide another scientific conference. CPHIA aims to create a continental space where evidence, political leadership, public-health implementation, financing, innovation, and partnerships can interact. Africa CDC describes the conference as an opportunity for African stakeholders to have open discussions about critical health challenges while sharing scientific breakthroughs and innovations capable of driving positive change. The broader goal is to translate evidence and innovation into health products, tools, policies, and adequately financed programmes. CPHIA 2026 Dates and Location Conference: 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa Dates: 23–27 November 2026 Location: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia Host city: Addis Ababa Expected attendance: More than 30,000 delegates Theme: Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from health dependency and vulnerability to ownership and resilience. Addis Ababa is also home to Africa CDC and the African Union headquarters, placing CPHIA 2026 in one of the continent s principal diplomatic and multilateral centres. Why CPHIA Matters for African Public Health The conference has evolved substantially since its first edition in 2021. Africa CDC describes CPHIA as a major platform for African health actors and champions to discuss issues affecting health across the continent and share scientific evidence that can support practical solutions. Its history includes: 2021: Inaugural virtual conference 2022: Kigali, Rwanda 2023: Lusaka, Zambia 2025: Durban, South Africa 2026: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia The inaugural 2021 edition attracted more than 12,000 virtual participants. The 2022 conference in Kigali recorded more than 14,000 in-person and virtual participants, the 2023 event in Lusaka recorded more than 35,000, and the 2025 Durban edition attracted more than 17,000 participants across virtual and physical formats. CPHIA 2026 Mission CPHIA’s mission is centered on bringing together African and international stakeholders to: Share knowledge Build partnerships Catalyse action Strengthen African health security Advance universal health coverage Promote locally driven solutions Strengthen continental solidarity Its vision is of a healthier, prosperous, and more self-reliant Africa supported by stronger health systems, local manufacturing capabilities, and a skilled health workforce. Core Pillars of CPHIA The conference identifies three broad pillars underpinning its work: Science and Innovation Scientific evidence is central to CPHIA. Researchers are given opportunities to present findings and connect scientific knowledge with decision-makers responsible for policy and implementation. Transformative Policies and Action The conference seeks to move discussions beyond identifying problems toward policies and programmes capable of generating change. Political Leadership for Impact Government leadership and political commitment are important components of strengthening health systems and ensuring that research and public-health priorities receive sustained attention and resources. What to Expect at CPHIA 2026 Africa CDC describes CPHIA 2026 as five days of discussions, research presentations, networking, innovation, and collaboration. The conference experience is expected to include six particularly prominent components. 1. High-Level Policy Dialogue CPHIA will bring participants into discussions involving: Heads of State and Government Ministers Global health leaders Members of the diplomatic community This gives the conference a significant policy dimension alongside its scientific programme. 2. Scientific Sessions The conference is expected to feature more than 100 sessions presenting research and innovations designed to contribute to evidence-based policies and action. Researchers whose abstracts are accepted may have opportunities to present their work through oral, poster, or electronic presentation formats. 3. Innovation, Financing and Investment CPHIA 2026 will provide opportunities to showcase health products, technologies, and innovations, with particular attention to African solutions. title: Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 in the UK: Fully Funded 10-Week Research Fellowship with £10,000 Stipend
summary: The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 is a fully funded, 10-week research fellowship in Cambridge, United Kingdom, designed for talented researchers, professionals, policymakers, and individuals from diverse academic and professional backgrounds who want to work on some of the most important challenges surrounding advanced artificial intelligence. The Winter 2027 cohort will begin on 18 January 2027 and will provide selected fellows with financial support, expert mentorship, research assistance, networking opportunities, and access to a community working at the intersection of AI safety, AI governance, technical research, and public policy . With a £10,000 stipend , visa support, meals during working hours, and travel expense coverage, the fellowship offers participants an opportunity to spend 10 weeks developing a substantial research project while working alongside experienced researchers and mentors in Cambridge. Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 at a Glance Opportunity: Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship Cohort: Winter 2027 Location: Cambridge, United Kingdom Duration: 10 weeks Start date: 18 January 2027 Stipend: £10,000 Funding: Fully funded Application deadline: 13 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Anywhere on Earth Minimum age: 18 years Application: Online Research areas: Technical AI Safety, AI Governance, and Technical AI Governance Mentorship: Yes Visa support: Yes Travel support: Yes Meals: Provided during working hours Potential continuation: 6+ month fully funded Research Scholars positions may be available to top fellows What Is the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship? The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship is a 10-week research programme hosted in Cambridge, UK. It is focused on helping talented individuals investigate ways of reducing risks associated with increasingly capable and autonomous AI systems. The programme brings together people from different disciplines and professional backgrounds. Rather than limiting applications to individuals with a particular degree, nationality, profession, or academic credential, ERA takes a talent-first approach . Participants are expected to develop a research project addressing important questions in frontier AI safety, AI governance, or technical mechanisms that can make AI governance more effective. The fellowship is particularly relevant as artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable and are being integrated into areas ranging from scientific research and cybersecurity to public administration, business, education, and national security. What Does the Fellowship Provide? One of the major attractions of the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship is that fellows are provided with extensive financial and professional support throughout the programme. 1. £10,000 Fellowship Stipend Selected fellows receive a £10,000 stipend for the 10-week fellowship. This financial support allows participants to dedicate substantial time to their research without having to treat the fellowship as an unpaid professional commitment. 2. Visa Support For international fellows who require permission to participate in the programme in the United Kingdom, ERA provides visa support . This is particularly important for applicants based outside the UK who want to participate in the in-person fellowship in Cambridge. 3. Travel Expense Coverage The fellowship also provides support for travel expenses , helping reduce the financial barriers associated with travelling to Cambridge for the programme. 4. Meal Provisions Fellows receive meal provisions during working hours , providing additional practical support during the 10-week programme. 5. Expert Mentorship Each fellow works closely with a mentor during the fellowship. Mentorship is an important component of the programme because participants are expected to develop and complete a meaningful research project. Mentors can provide guidance on research questions, methodology, project development, academic direction, and the broader implications of the fellow s work. ERA notes that mentors differ between cohorts. Fellows are matched with mentors after acceptance according to their research interests and needs. Previous ERA mentors have included researchers and experts associated with organisations across academia, government, industry, and AI safety. 6. Research Management Support Fellows receive dedicated research management support throughout their projects. This support is intended to help participants become stronger researchers and policymakers in the AI safety and governance space. The fellowship s alumni have gone on to publish research in prominent academic venues, including conferences such as NeurIPS. 7. Cambridge Research Community Participants become part of a community of people working on difficult questions related to advanced AI. During the fellowship, fellows have access to a dedicated desk space at ERA s Cambridge office and participate in regular social events and community activities. This creates opportunities to exchange ideas, receive feedback, collaborate, and build professional relationships. 8. Networking and Career Development ERA also helps fellows develop the skills, expertise, and networks necessary for careers in AI safety and AI policy. The organisation can facilitate introductions to relevant organisations and professionals working in the field. In exceptional cases, ERA may also provide additional financial assistance to support particularly impactful career transitions. 9. Potential Long-Term Research Opportunities The fellowship can also serve as a pathway to longer-term research. Top-performing fellows may have the opportunity to continue their work through ERA s Research Scholars programme , which offers six months or longer of full-time funded positions . This means that the 10-week fellowship can potentially become the beginning of a much longer research career in AI safety or governance. Who Can Apply for the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship? One of the most distinctive aspects of this fellowship is its broad eligibility policy. Anyone aged 18 or older can apply. ERA describes the programme as talent-first and states that it cares about much more than conventional credentials. There are no formal eligibility restrictions beyond being at least 18 years old . Applicants therefore do not necessarily need to come from a traditional computer science or artificial intelligence background. The programme welcomes people with different forms of expertise, provided they have the ability, motivation, and potential to contribute meaningfully to the mission of reducing risks associated with advanced AI. Who Is Particularly Encouraged to Apply? Although the fellowship is open broadly, it may be especially valuable for the following groups. Researchers at Any Career Stage Researchers can apply if they want to: Apply their existing expertise to high-priority AI safety or governance questions. Explore a new research direction. Work across disciplinary boundaries. Develop research relevant to advanced AI systems. Redirect an existing research programme toward frontier AI challenges. The programme is not restricted to senior academics. Researchers at different stages of their careers may be considered. Professionals from Technical and Policy Fields Professionals working in areas such as: Technology Computer science Artificial intelligence Public policy Government National security Security studies Law Economics Research Governance Regulation Other relevant disciplines may find the fellowship particularly valuable. The programme provides an opportunity to apply existing professional expertise to emerging problems associated with increasingly capable AI systems. People Redirecting Their Research Careers The fellowship can also suit individuals who already have a research agenda but want to shift their work toward advanced AI safety and governance. For example, someone with expertise in economics, cybersecurity, law, international relations, public administration, or computer science could use the fellowship to investigate how that discipline can contribute to managing risks from frontier AI. Individuals with Distinctive Domain Expertise ERA is also interested in applicants who bring unusual or underrepresented perspectives. An applicant does not necessarily need to be an AI specialist if they possess expertise that could improve society s understanding of advanced AI risks or contribute to developing effective solutions. What Will Fellows Research? During the fellowship, participants develop and complete a research project focused on technical and/or governance measures for mitigating risks posed by frontier AI systems . Fellows receive support from: ERA research managers Individual mentors ERA s wider institutional network Researchers and experts from relevant organisations ERA supports research across the full range of frontier AI governance and technical AI safety. Its wider research network includes experts associated with organisations such as the University of Cambridge, UK AI Security Institute, Centre for the Governance of AI, RAND Corporation, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic , among others. The research programme is divided broadly into three streams. 1. Technical AI Safety The technical stream focuses on understanding increasingly capable AI systems and developing methods to ensure that humans can maintain meaningful control and oversight. As AI systems become more autonomous, researchers need to understand what these systems can do, how they behave, what capabilities they may develop, and how to prevent harmful or unpredictable outcomes. ERA supports technical research in areas including: AI evaluations Interpretability Robustness Alignment AI control Dangerous capability detection Model behaviour monitoring Safeguards Human oversight AI system reliability Research may involve investigating how to measure or elicit potentially dangerous capabilities, understanding the internal workings of AI models, designing stronger safeguards, monitoring model behaviour, and developing techniques for controlling systems whose objectives may not fully align with those of their operators. The programme is also interested in emerging challenges such as: Detecting deceptive or strategically evasive AI behaviour. Controlling AI systems capable of automating parts of AI research and development. Accelerating alignment research across the LLM training stack. Developing safeguards that remain effective as AI models become increasingly capable. The overall objective is to contribute to the development of AI systems that can remain subject to effective human oversight while incorporating appropriate safeguards against harmful or unpredictable behaviour. 2. AI Governance The governance stream focuses on how governments, companies, international institutions, and other organisations should manage increasingly capable AI systems. As frontier AI becomes more powerful, decisions regarding its development and deployment become increasingly consequential. Effective governance requires institutions that can: Understand rapidly changing AI risks. Develop credible rules and safeguards. Hold powerful AI developers accountable. Coordinate across national borders. Respond to emerging technological developments. Build effective regulatory systems. ERA supports research in areas such as: Regulatory design Regulatory implementation Frontier AI safety frameworks Corporate governance Accountability International coordination AI policy Institutional capacity Researchers in this stream may investigate how governments and other institutions can develop governance systems that keep pace with technological progress. Potential research questions may involve increasingly autonomous AI agents, international coordination, frontier AI regulation, and the development of security and verification systems for advanced AI. The broader goal is to help institutions adapt as AI capabilities and associated risks change. 3. Technical AI Governance Technical AI governance sits at the intersection of AI technology, governance, regulation, measurement, and verification. The central idea is that effective AI governance cannot depend entirely on companies voluntarily reporting what their systems can do or how they were developed. Governments and other stakeholders need reliable technical mechanisms for determining: What AI systems are capable of. How much computing power they use. Where systems are deployed. How systems are developed. Whether regulatory requirements are being followed. Whether claims made by AI developers can be independently verified. ERA therefore supports research involving: Compute governance AI auditing AI monitoring Hardware-enabled verification Technical standards Measurement Privacy-preserving verification AI system auditing Potential research could explore how regulators can identify AI systems that cross important risk thresholds, how hardware and computing infrastructure can enable verification while protecting privacy, and how increasingly autonomous systems can be monitored. This field is particularly important because policymakers may create effective regulations but struggle to implement them if they lack the technical infrastructure needed to measure compliance. ERA s objective is to help develop governance systems based on credible measurement, verification, and enforcement rather than relying solely on trust or self-reporting. Why Is the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship Important? The rapid development of frontier AI has created a growing need for people who can understand both the opportunities and risks associated with increasingly capable systems. AI safety is not solely a computer science problem. It involves questions concerning: Public policy Economics International relations Law Security Ethics Governance Computer science Engineering Institutional design Regulation This makes interdisciplinary expertise increasingly valuable. The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship provides an environment in which individuals from different backgrounds can bring their knowledge to emerging questions surrounding advanced AI. For someone considering a career in AI safety, AI governance, technology policy, or related research, the fellowship can provide an opportunity to gain specialised experience while building connections with researchers and institutions working in the field. Application Process for the Winter 2027 Fellowship Applications for the Winter 2027 Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship are currently open . The selection process consists of several stages. Stage 1: Written Application The first stage primarily consists of short essay questions. ERA estimates that applicants should spend approximately two hours completing this stage. The written application is an important opportunity for candidates to demonstrate their thinking, motivation, research ability, and potential contribution to AI safety or governance. Applicants should therefore approach the essays carefully rather than treating them as a simple administrative form. Stage 2: First Interview Following the written application stage, approximately the top 20% of candidates will be invited to first-round interviews. These interviews are scheduled to take place in late September 2026 . Candidates should be prepared to discuss their interests, experience, reasoning, and potential research directions. Stage 3: Second Interview Applicants who are particularly promising after the first interview may be invited to a shorter second-round interview. When candidates are invited to this stage, ERA will also contact their references. Second-round interviews are expected to take place in early October 2026 . Stage 4: Offers and Research Development Following the selection process, successful applicants will receive acceptance offers. After offers are made, ERA will work with the selected fellows to develop their project ideas and match them with appropriate mentors. This means applicants do not necessarily need to arrive with a completely finalised research proposal. The fellowship provides an environment in which project ideas can be refined with support from research managers and mentors. Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship Deadline The application deadline for the Winter 2027 Fellowship is: 13 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m. Anywhere on Earth (AoE). Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their applications. Because the deadline is expressed in Anywhere on Earth time, applicants should verify the corresponding deadline in their local time zone and submit well in advance. How to Apply for the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship Interested applicants can submit their application through the official application form. Applicants should carefully review the application questions and provide clear, thoughtful responses demonstrating their suitability for the fellowship. Tips for Preparing a Strong Application Although the fellowship is talent-first and does not impose traditional academic eligibility requirements, applicants should still demonstrate why they are capable of making a meaningful contribution. 1. Clearly Explain Your Interest in Advanced AI Show that you understand why AI safety and governance matter and explain what motivates you to work on these issues. 2. Connect Your Existing Expertise to AI You do not necessarily need an AI degree. Instead, explain how your current knowledge could contribute to AI safety, governance, or technical AI governance. For example, a lawyer could explore AI regulation, an economist could investigate AI incentives and governance, a cybersecurity professional could examine AI security, while a political scientist could investigate international coordination. 3. Demonstrate Strong Research Thinking The fellowship is fundamentally research-oriented. Applicants should demonstrate an ability to identify important questions, think critically, analyse evidence, and develop useful approaches to complex problems. 4. Identify Potential Research Directions While a fully developed proposal may not be required, having some ideas about the problems you would like to investigate can strengthen your application. Think about questions that are: Important Relevant to frontier AI Researchable Potentially impactful Connected to your existing expertise 5. Highlight Your Distinctive Perspective ERA specifically welcomes people with distinctive domain expertise and perspectives. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that they must compete by presenting themselves as conventional AI researchers. Your unique professional or academic background may be one of your greatest strengths. 6. Take the Essay Questions Seriously The written application is the first major stage of selection. Because the programme expects applicants to spend around two hours on the essays, candidates should dedicate sufficient time to developing thoughtful and well-structured responses. 7. Prepare for Interviews Candidates selected for interviews should be ready to explain: Why they are interested in AI safety or governance. What research questions interest them. How their existing expertise could contribute. How they approach difficult and uncertain problems. What they hope to accomplish during the fellowship. Location and Fellowship Experience The fellowship is hosted in Cambridge, United Kingdom . Fellows will have dedicated desk space at the ERA office and will participate in community activities and social events. The in-person environment provides opportunities to interact with other researchers and professionals while working on individual projects. Cambridge also provides a strong academic and research environment, making it a particularly relevant location for individuals interested in advanced technology, public policy, and interdisciplinary research. Who Should Consider Applying? The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship may be particularly suitable for someone who: Wants to transition into AI safety research. Is already conducting research and wants to explore advanced AI questions. Works in technology or engineering. Has expertise in public policy or government. Works in law or regulation. Has a background in economics. Works in national security or cybersecurity. Wants to develop expertise in AI governance. Has interdisciplinary research interests. Possesses distinctive expertise that could contribute to understanding AI risks. Wants to build a professional network in AI safety and governance. Is interested in pursuing a longer-term research career. Because the fellowship has no formal eligibility restrictions beyond the minimum age requirement, applicants should not automatically exclude themselves because they do not have a traditional AI background. APPLY HERE International Eligibility and Nationality The fellowship states that anyone can apply , provided they are 18 years or older . There is no stated restriction limiting applications to a particular race, nationality, country, or continent. Therefore, applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, and other parts of the world may apply, subject to meeting the programme s general requirements and being able to participate in the fellowship in Cambridge. The fellowship s broad approach means that applicants from countries across the Global South and Global North can potentially be considered. International applicants should also take into account the practical requirements associated with travelling to and participating in a 10-week programme in the United Kingdom. ERA states that it provides visa support and travel expense coverage for fellows. Visit HERE to learn more about the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 in the UK. Key Reasons to Consider the Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship The fellowship combines several elements that can be difficult to access through conventional research opportunities: A £10,000 stipend for the 10-week programme. Visa support for eligible international participants. Travel expense coverage. Meals during working hours. One-to-one mentorship. Dedicated research management support. Access to a Cambridge-based research community. Networking opportunities across AI safety and governance. Opportunities to develop research that can potentially lead to academic publication. Potential access to 6+ month funded Research Scholars positions for top fellows. The combination of financial support, mentorship, research experience, and professional networking makes the programme particularly relevant for individuals seeking to build a long-term career in AI safety or governance. Conclusion The Cambridge ERA:AI Fellowship 2027 offers an intensive 10-week opportunity for talented individuals to work on some of the world s most important emerging questions surrounding advanced artificial intelligence.
